description: How dependency versions move in every 2Fivers project. A web-only project's renovate.json extends this preset; a project with an Expo app extends :mobile, which extends this one.

The split that carries the design: TOOLING merges itself, everything else waits for a human. Tooling is the set below that `pnpm check` exercises in full -- if the linter, type checker, dead-code check and tests all run green on the new version, the change is proven by the same gate that proves any commit. Runtime dependencies are different: CI proves that they build and that the unit tests pass, not that the site works. So they stay manual, and they come once a month instead of every week.

Where a project deploys on every push to main, an automerged pull request is a deploy. The safeguards are therefore what precedes the merge: every check green, the two-day minimumReleaseAge here, and pnpm's own minimumReleaseAge. Note that tooling does reach the build: typescript, @types/node and vitest are installed while the image is made and `next build` type-checks with typescript -- they do not end up in the served bundle, but they run while it is made.

minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour is timestamp-optional because under the default, timestamp-required, an update whose release carries no timestamp is held as pending forever rather than aged. Here that is every SHA pin and digest bump of a GitHub Action, which would sit with renovate/stability-days 'Updates have not met minimum release age requirement' for that reason alone, so the monthly github actions group would quietly stop delivering. npm and Docker Hub releases carry timestamps and keep the two-day wait; Renovate logs a WARN for each release it lets through unaged.
Renovate merges by itself once the checks are green, so automerge needs neither a human click per pull request nor GitHub's own auto-merge.

Renovate works at night: every schedule here is 02:00-06:00 Stockholm time, and so are automerges. The organisation's CI runs on two self-hosted slots, and in the daytime a burst of Renovate rebases queued a release behind six dependency pull requests. The window is four hours wide because Mend runs an active repository every four hours; a one-hour window would be missed on most nights. updateNotScheduled is false so that rebases stay inside the window too: outside it Renovate leaves its open branches alone, and a push to main during the day no longer rebases every open pull request. A branch that is wanted sooner is rebased by ticking its box in the pull request. Security fixes open at any hour once two days old and merge themselves inside this window (vulnerabilityAlerts below). The branches that merge themselves are the exceptions to the daytime rule: the lock file maintenance branch (lockFileMaintenance below) and the weekly tooling and expo groups (tooling below, and :mobile) are rebased when main moves, because a branch that is rebased only inside the window is never merged in it. Renovate merges at most one branch per project in each run, so they queue: security fixes first, then the lock file, then the weekly groups (prPriority).

vulnerabilityAlerts.description: Renovate is the CVE channel for DIRECT dependencies; for transitive ones it is lockFileMaintenance below. It reads the repository's Dependabot alerts and the OSV database and opens a pull request outside the schedule, with the lockfile updated. Dependabot's own security updates do not work in a pnpm workspace: they rewrite package.json and leave pnpm-lock.yaml alone, so every one fails `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` with ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE and the fix never lands. Dependabot security updates should therefore be off in pnpm repositories; the alerts stay on, because this reads them. TWO DAYS OLD FIRST, the same minimumReleaseAge as every other update. Renovate's own default for a vulnerability fix is no wait at all, and with it a version published together with an advisory that names it as the fix would merge that night and leave with the next release: the one path into a project with nothing aging in front of it. The wait costs almost nothing, because a fixed version is nearly always older than that by the time its advisory arrives (homelab-docs ADR 0121). While the fix is younger, Renovate creates no branch (internalChecksFilter strict) and lists it under 'Pending Status Checks' on the Dependency Dashboard. Ticking it there opens the pull request at once, for a human to merge; automerge still waits for the age. Renovate also writes the fixed version into pnpm's minimumReleaseAgeExclude, which after two days exempts it from nothing pnpm's one-day wait would still hold. AUTOMERGED once every check is green, inside automergeSchedule like every other automerge: Renovate skips `schedule` for a vulnerability fix and still checks automergeSchedule, so a fix that comes of age in the afternoon merges that night. Merging deploys nothing; a published web-v* release does, made by a person or by the release bot. A security fix can be a runtime dependency, which `pnpm check` does not prove the way it proves tooling; the gate is the same one that proves any commit, every check green, and a human can still stop a fix by closing its pull request.

lockFileMaintenance.description: TRANSITIVE dependencies -- the only path a fix in one has. GitHub's dependency graph reads only the first YAML document of pnpm 12's pnpm-lock.yaml, the one that holds pnpm itself, so no transitive package in a pnpm repository ever raises a Dependabot alert; and vulnerabilityAlerts and osvVulnerabilityAlerts act only on the dependencies Renovate extracts from package.json. Lock file maintenance regenerates pnpm-lock.yaml instead, which moves every transitive package to the newest version its parent's range allows, with or without an advisory. The direct dependencies are pinned exactly, so it does not move them. EVERY NIGHT: the branch is created inside the window. updateNotScheduled is true here, unlike the top level, because Renovate never automerges a branch outside its schedule when updateNotScheduled is false: a branch that a daytime push put behind main would be rebased in the next window and merged in none. With true it is rebased when main moves, like a security fix, and merges in the next window in which it is green and has no new commit (automergeSchedule). AUTOMERGED, so no human stands between an npm publish and the nightly release of a transitive version. What does: pnpm's own minimumReleaseAge in pnpm-workspace.yaml -- Renovate's two days above do not apply to lock file maintenance -- allowBuilds, which fails the install on a build script nobody reviewed, and every check green. A project whose direct dependencies carry ranges instead of exact pins turns this off in its own renovate.json, or it would move them too.

packageRules.description: Every npm dependency that no later rule claims shares one monthly pull request per project, instead of one per package. Later rules override this groupName.
next and its scoped packages release in lockstep.
Reached in web-only projects. In a project with an Expo app the SDK pins these, and :mobile freezes them.

pnpm itself, from package.json's packageManager (the one CI reads) and, in a project with an app, apps/mobile/eas.json (see :mobile). Its own pull request, so that a pnpm problem does not hold back the runtime dependencies.

The Node patch and minor: the Dockerfile's base tag and, in a project with an app, build.base.node in apps/mobile/eas.json (see :mobile), in one pull request so that the web image and the mobile build stay on the same Node. The major is disabled below.

GitHub Actions monthly in one pull request. Not automerged: the login, push and bump steps run only on main, so a pull request cannot prove an action that only those steps use. Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA with the version as a comment (helpers:pinGitHubActionDigests above): a tag like @v4 can be moved by whoever controls the action's repository, a SHA cannot, and with the digest pinned Renovate also sees the minors and patches that @v4 used to hide. The first run opens a one-off pull request that pins every action.
Our own reusable workflows, called as 2Fivers/workflows/...@v1. The floating v1 tag is the design: moving it is how a fix reaches every project at once, so neither a pin nor a bump is wanted here.

TOOLING -- weekly, and it merges itself once every check is green. Each name here is a devDependency that `pnpm check` runs in full and that is not part of the served bundle (see the top-level description for why that is not the same as never touching the build). typescript and oxlint-tsgolint (7.0.2NNN tracks TypeScript 7.0.2) must move together, which the shared group guarantees. Add a name only if `pnpm check` exercises it and it does not ship. CREATED on Monday night, MERGED on a later night: updateNotScheduled is true here, unlike the top level, for the reason given under lockFileMaintenance. With false the group was rebased every Monday night and merged on none, because a daytime push since the Monday before had put it behind main (homelab-docs ADR 0107). prPriority -1 sorts it after the lock file maintenance branch, which carries the transitive security fixes; without it the group would sort first as a minor or patch and take the lock file's one merge of the night.

Majors are decisions. They are listed on the Dependency Dashboard and get a branch only when someone ticks the box -- which also keeps them from spending Actions minutes on a pull request that is red until a human ports the code. Placed after the groups so it overrides their automerge.

The Node major is a decision taken by hand in five places at once (engines, @types/node, node-version in both workflows, the Dockerfile's base tag, build.base.node in eas.json), so no tool proposes it.
